styleWhy: The scam happens on a phone screen, so showing that screen step by step (the text, the tap, the fake page, the form) is the clearest way to show it.

copy.idea: A fake 'delivery problem' text sends you to a copycat page that asks for a small fee and takes your card details. The video walks through each step on a phone and shows the signs that give it away.
copy.hook: Americans reported $470 million lost to text scams in 2024, and fake package-delivery texts were the most reported text scam that year.
copy.body:
A text arrives: your parcel is on hold, pay a small redelivery fee. It comes from an unknown number, it pushes you to hurry, and the link looks odd.

Tap it and a page opens that looks just like a courier's site, but the address in the bar isn't theirs.

It asks for a tiny fee, so you type in your card number, expiry date and security code, then press Pay.

Those details go straight to the scammers, who can use the card themselves.

How to beat it: don't tap. Check with the company using a website or number you know is real, not the one in the text. Forward the text to 7726, then delete it.

facts.text: “In 2024, people reported $470 million in losses to these scams, more than five times the 2020 number.”
facts.source: FTC Data Spotlight, 'Top text scams of 2024', 14 Apr 2025 — https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/data-visualizations/data-spotlight/2025/04/top-text-scams-2024

facts.text: “Messages about package deliveries, usually from someone pretending to be from the U.S. Postal Service, were the most reported text scam last year.” (last year = 2024)
facts.source: FTC Data Spotlight, 'Top text scams of 2024', 14 Apr 2025 — https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/data-visualizations/data-spotlight/2025/04/top-text-scams-2024

facts.text: Scam texts often claim a problem with a delivery and include a link; you shouldn't click links in unexpected texts.
facts.source: FTC Consumer Advice, 'How To Recognize and Report Spam Text Messages' — https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/how-recognize-and-report-spam-text-messages

facts.text: “Copy the message and forward it to 7726 (SPAM). This helps your wireless provider spot and block similar messages in the future.”
facts.source: FTC Consumer Advice, 'How To Recognize and Report Spam Text Messages' — https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/how-recognize-and-report-spam-text-messages

facts.text: “If you think the message might be real, contact the company using a phone number or website you know is real. Not the information in the text message.”
facts.source: FTC Consumer Advice, 'How To Recognize and Report Spam Text Messages' — https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/how-recognize-and-report-spam-text-messages

facts.text: Illustrative, not sourced: the $1.99 fee, the sender number, the parcel-redeliver.info address, the pay page, the card and the charges are made up for the video; no real courier brand or logo is shown.

shots.title: Hook: the text lands
shots.show: The phone (recurring) fills the frame on a dark lock screen. A notification drops from the top: 'Your parcel is on hold'. Above the phone, a big red counter rolls up to $470M and lands with a bounce, under the line 'lost to text scams in 2024'; the kicker reads 'US 2024 · #1 reported: parcel texts'; behind it, faint copies of the same notification stack up and pile across the screen (illustrative), filling the frame.
shots.motion: Notification slides down with a buzz shake; the counter rolls from 0 to $470M and bounces; ghost notifications keep stacking in the background until the cut.
shots.source: FTC Data Spotlight, 'Top text scams of 2024', 14 Apr 2025 (US, 2024 reports)

shots.title: Red flags in the text
shots.show: The phone opens to the messages app: the fake text bubble (recurring) reads 'Your parcel is on hold. Pay a $1.99 redelivery fee within 24h: parcel-redeliver.info/xyz'. Three red flags pin on in turn: a circle around the unknown number at the top ('Unknown number'), an underline on '24h' ('Rush'), a box around the link ('Odd link').
shots.text: Unknown number, a rush, an odd link
shots.motion: The phone zooms gently in; each red ring draws itself around its part with a small pop, its label sliding out to the side.
shots.source: FTC, 'How To Recognize and Report Spam Text Messages'

shots.title: The tap and the fake page
shots.show: A finger icon taps the link; a ripple spreads. The browser opens on the fake pay page (recurring): a courier-style header, a parcel icon and 'Delivery fee: $1.99'. The address bar zooms up and turns red: 'parcel-redeliver.info' with the label 'Not the courier's site'.
shots.text: The page looks real. The address isn't.
shots.motion: Tap ripple, then the page slides up over the messages; the address bar lifts out of the phone, scales up, and a red outline pulses around it.

shots.title: Card details typed in
shots.show: The fake pay page (recurring) scrolls to a card form. The fields fill in one after another as if typed: card number (shown as 4•••• •••• •••• 1234), expiry, security code. The finger taps a 'Pay $1.99' button.
shots.text: A $1.99 fee for your full card
shots.motion: Each field lights blue as the cursor enters, characters type in with a blink; the Pay button presses down with a tap ripple.

shots.title: Where your details go
shots.show: Hop path: the card form on the phone shrinks to the left; the three filled fields peel off as red data chips and fly along a dotted line to a hooded-figure server icon on the right labelled 'Scammers'. Under it, a receipt list drops in with unknown charges (labelled 'illustrative').
shots.text: Your card goes straight to the scammers
shots.motion: The dotted path draws itself left to right; chips travel along it one by one and land in the server, which glows red; charge rows slide in below.

shots.title: How to beat it
shots.show: Back to the phone with the fake text bubble (recurring). The link is crossed out in red ('Don't tap'). Then two green steps: a saved courier site the viewer already knows (not the text's link) opens on a tracking screen ('Use a site you know is real'), and the text is forwarded to 7726 with a green check, then swiped away as deleted.
shots.text: Don't tap. Use a known site. Forward to 7726.
shots.motion: The red line strikes through the link; a green card slides in for each step with a tick; the message bubble flies off left in the delete swipe.
shots.source: FTC, 'How To Recognize and Report Spam Text Messages'

shots.title: End card
shots.show: The phone sits at the center with a calm lock screen and a green shield over it; the old fake notification drops in, turns grey and dissolves. Around it, short labels orbit: 'Unknown number', 'Rush', 'Odd link'.
shots.motion: The shield snaps shut like a lock; labels circle slowly; the notification fades to nothing.

recurring.design: A large modern phone, centred, filling about 70% of the frame height, graphite body with thin bezels; the caption sits above it, the source line small below it. Red marks scam elements, green marks safe actions, blue marks the active field or tap.
